seo.title: Karmic tail 18 3 12 compatibility: the myth of the other half
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 3 12 compatibility: what The Moon, The Empress and The Hanged Man mean for a couple, read through Plato's myth of the other half.

title: Karmic Tail 18-3-12 in Compatibility: The Moon, The Empress and The Hanged Man
short: The idea of an "other half" is nearly two and a half thousand years old, and few people remember how the story it comes from ends. The halves who found each other embraced — and were dying of hunger, "because they did not like to do anything apart". The karmic tail 18-3-12 in compatibility tells this myth in three cards: The Moon is the wish to find one's other half, The Empress is the road on which the embrace turns into shared work and a home, and The Hanged Man is the couple's main task: not to freeze in the embrace.

sections.h2: The speech that a fit of hiccups delayed
paragraphs: Plato's Symposium is the story of one evening at the house of the tragic poet Agathon, who was celebrating a victory in a theatre contest; it was written in the fourth century BC. The guests agreed not to drink hard but to take turns praising Eros. When the turn came to the comic poet Aristophanes — the same man who had mocked Socrates in The Clouds — he "had the hiccough, and was obliged to change turns with Eryximachus". The speech that gave us the "other half" began only after Aristophanes had sneezed himself clear.

His story goes like this. Once, people were round: four hands, four feet, two faces on a single neck. There were three sexes, each with its own parent: "the man was originally the child of the sun, the woman of the earth, and the man-woman of the moon, which is made up of sun and earth". The round people were so strong that they tried to scale heaven. Zeus chose not to destroy them and found another way: "I will cut them in two". Apollo drew the skin together over the belly like a purse, tied the knot we call the navel, and left a few wrinkles "as a memorial of the primeval state".

Then comes the part that is usually left out. The severed halves rushed to each other. "Throwing their arms about one another, entwined in mutual embraces, longing to grow into one", they stayed that way. "They were on the point of dying from hunger and self-neglect, because they did not like to do anything apart." When one died, the survivor sought another and clung to it. The race was perishing, and Zeus, taking pity, devised a second remedy: he rearranged their bodies so that the embrace would bear fruit — children, or at least satisfaction, after which people would "rest, and go their ways to the business of life".

At the end Aristophanes sets up a thought experiment. Suppose Hephaestus came with his tools to two lovers lying together and asked: "What do you people want of one another?" They would be unable to say. So the smith would make the offer himself: "Do you desire to be wholly one; always day and night to be in one another's company? for if this is what you desire, I am ready to melt you into one and let you grow together, so that being two you shall become one". Not one of them, Aristophanes assures us, would refuse. And he sums up in words that have outlived every century since: "the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love".

Lay the three cards of the tail side by side and the myth sorts itself across them. The children of the Moon, who long for the whole and cannot explain what they want, are the entry. Zeus's second remedy, which turns the embrace into fruit and sends people back to work, is the middle. The two frozen in the embrace, and the smith ready to make it permanent, are the main task.

The first clue is in the numbers. The 18-3-12 tail occurs in about one couple in 679 (0.147%), ranking 79th of the 97 couple tails. It is built in only three ways, and the main one is striking: in 77% of cases both partners have the same personal karmic tail, 9-15-6. The worked example on the site is two people born on the same day, 14 May 1976.

Each point of a couple's tail is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices. When two identical halves are added, each card simply doubles. The Hermit and The Hermit (9 + 9) give The Moon. The Devil and The Devil (15 + 15 = 30 → 3) give The Empress. The Lovers and The Lovers (6 + 6) give The Hanged Man. **Two matching halves do not restore the original sphere: their sum produces three cards that appear in neither partner's tail.** An 18-3-12 couple is not one person multiplied by two but a third being with a plot of its own.

In the remaining couples the plot is the same but assembled differently. In 12% of cases the personal tails 9-12-3 and 9-18-9 are added: The Moon, The Empress and The Hanged Man already lie in the two tails separately, except that in one partner The Hanged Man comes before The Empress, and in the couple's tail they swap places. In another 11%, 12-16-4 and 6-14-8 are added — entirely different cards that still converge on the same three numbers.

The second clue is the centre. In every couple with this tail, the centre of the couple's matrix holds The Lovers, 6. The couple's centre is its shared atmosphere, what lives inside the union and is not put on show. In the myth, this is Eros himself, "the desire and pursuit of the whole". Wen calls The Lovers a card of "partnership with one other person" and allows that it could relate to the sign Gemini. At the heart of a union most often built by doubles stands a card linked with the Twins.

sections.h2: The Moon at the entry: children of the Moon and an unspoken contract
paragraphs: M is the "Entry to the task". It is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. This wish is how the two enter their task, and because it stands on the line of tasks, the same wish can turn into resistance.

The 18-3-12 tail has The Moon at the entry — the very Moon that Aristophanes made the parent of people composed of two different halves. One word ties the card to the myth more tightly than any interpretation. Benebell Wen describes the theme of The Moon like this: "constant change, duality, and dichotomy". The Greek "dichotomy" is built from "dicha", "in two", and "temno", "I cut". These are exactly the words of Plato's Zeus: "διατεμῶ δίχα ἕκαστον" — "I will cut each of them in two", and then "ἔτεμνε τοὺς ἀνθρώπους δίχα" — "he cut men in two". And in astronomy, dichotomy is the phase when exactly half of the Moon's disc is lit. **The Moon at the entry to this tail is a half-moon.**

What do the halves want? Aristophanes admits they cannot say. The lovers spend their whole lives together, "yet they could not explain what they desire of one another"; the soul of each has "only a dark and doubtful presentiment" of what it wants. This is the common language of the 18-3-12 tail — a language of guesses. At their first meeting the two recognise each other as if they had always known each other. They finish each other's sentences, talk until dawn, and have their own words and jokes that no one else understands. The Moon in a couple is fine intuition: the partner is first of all a friend, understanding needs no explanation, each has a space of their own, and still the two keep discovering something new in each other for years.

Each of us, says Aristophanes, "like a flat fish, is but the indenture of a man, and he is always looking for his other half". Plato's word is "symbolon": half of a broken tally that a host and a guest split between them, so that years later they could join the halves and recognise each other. Through Latin it gave us the word "symbol". Benjamin Jowett's translation names the half even more precisely — an indenture, a contract written twice on one sheet and cut apart along a jagged line. Recognition by a matching break is what the couple feels at the entry. And that is why this point governs agreements.

The contract between halves has a flaw: no one has ever read it aloud. Each is sure the other already knows the terms. This is where The Moon at the entry turns into resistance. "If you're my other half, you'll guess" — and instead of a conversation, the reading of silences begins. One imagines what the other thought and takes offence at what was imagined. The image formed in the first months does not survive daylight: "I thought you were just like me". Adjusting to the partner builds up and one day comes out as irritation. Taking a step without the other's approval becomes impossible. Waite calls The Moon "life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit". A half that sees its own reflection in the other lives exactly like that.

sections.h2: The Empress in the middle: Zeus's second remedy
paragraphs: N is the "Middle of the task". Lisovskaya gives this point no meaning of its own: it is an addition to the main task. On the site it is read as the road — what the couple does and goes through on the way from the wish at the entry to the task at the end. This is the product's reading, not a statement of the book.

The Empress stands in the middle of the 18-3-12 tail — and in the middle of the myth stands her work. Look at what kills the halves. In Greek it is "argia", idleness, and the word is built from "a-", "without", and "ergon", "work": literally work-less-ness. Zeus's remedy sends people back "to their works", and the original uses the same root: ἐπὶ τὰ ἔργα. **The trouble and the way out are named by one word.** And Waite's divinatory list for The Empress opens with "Fruitfulness, action, initiative" — exactly what the embracing halves lacked.

Waite adds a formula to The Empress that reads like a continuation of The Moon: she has been, he writes, "correctly described as desire and the wings thereof". At the entry the couple has a desire that cannot name itself. In the middle this desire gets wings — direction, work, fruit. For Wen, The Empress is "the card of fruition" and suggests "an incredible gift for harnessing interpersonal relationships to yield success and harmony".

The Symposium itself supplies the second half of the answer. After Aristophanes, Socrates takes the floor and retells the lesson of a wise woman from Mantinea, Diotima. She argues with the myth of the halves directly: "you hear people say that lovers are seeking for their other half; but I say that they are seeking neither for the half of themselves, nor for the whole, unless the half or the whole be also a good". What, then, does love want? "The object which they have in view is birth in beauty, whether of body or soul." "All men are bringing to the birth in their bodies and in their souls," says Diotima, and the children she means are not only children: the poems of Homer and Hesiod, the laws of Lycurgus and Solon. And she adds what matters most for a couple: the lover "in company with him tends that which he brings forth; and they are married by a far nearer tie and have a closer friendship than those who beget mortal children". The union is held together not by the embrace but by a third thing — what the two have brought into being and are raising together.

This is what The Empress in the middle of the tail means: the couple's road runs through making something shared. A rented flat that the two turn into a home. A country plot where something gets planted every summer. A shared business, a shared renovation, a dog, a book, a kitchen where every dish has a story, children if the couple has them. The Empress in a couple stands for comfort, care, joint projects and growth through shared goals — with one important condition: each must keep a calling of their own. The third thing does not replace the two. It stands between them, like a table at which they sit facing each other rather than wrapped around each other.

Diotima also described the minus of the middle, in one sentence about a being that carries fruit with nothing beautiful nearby: it "shrinks, turns away, curls up and does not give birth, but holds what it has conceived and carries it with difficulty" (206d, our translation from the Greek). In a couple it looks like this. Plans stay plans for years. The home is always "being got ready". One partner pulls the shared project while the other waits. Money is feast or famine. One grows, the other stays where they are, and a quiet competition begins between them. Mum and the relatives decide for the two of them, and the couple never quite becomes a family of its own.

sections.h2: The Hanged Man as the main task: the offer of Hephaestus
paragraphs: D is the "Main task". It is the main point of the tail: the couple's chief problems and trials. It is read mostly through the minus — what is not working for the two and what they have to learn.

The Hanged Man in the main task is the halves from the middle of the myth, frozen in an embrace. They do not quarrel and they do not part. They simply stop doing anything apart, and that turns out to be enough to perish. The Hanged Man is the card of suspended life: all the figure on this card can do is hang. In a couple this looks not like a tragedy but like silence.

Five years in, neither remembers what they liked doing on their own. Friends first became "ours", then disappeared. An important decision — a move, a wedding, a new job — hangs for years: each waits for the other to want it first, and "we'll decide together" turns into "nobody decided". Lisovskaya notes of The Hanged Man in a couple that such partners take a long time to enter a relationship and need a push from outside to marry. Sometimes one holds everything together: remembers, organises, rescues, and hears reproaches in return, yet cannot leave, because "without me it will all fall apart". Sometimes the picture is perfect outside and heavy inside, and decisions are made "because that's how it should be" and "what will people say". And there is a harsh version: two people entwined against the whole world, where everyone around is to blame — and when there is no one left outside to blame, the pressure turns inward.

Hephaestus does not appear in this scene by chance. Aristophanes' listeners knew from the Odyssey how the lame smith had once already chained two people to a bed. He forged an invisible net for Ares and Aphrodite, so strong that, in Samuel Butler's translation, they "could neither get up nor stir hand or foot". The gods roared with laughter, and Hermes admitted he would gladly be bound "though there were three times as many chains", if only he could lie beside golden Aphrodite. In the Symposium, Hephaestus offers the same net — only now the lovers ask for it themselves. Aristophanes honestly includes the smith's question that usually gets skipped: "I ask whether this is what you lovingly desire, and whether you are satisfied to attain this?"

**The trap of the 18-3-12 tail is that it is pleasant.** A frozen couple feels fine, so the standstill is hard to notice: no one suffers, things simply stop happening. The main task is to see the union from the outside. Wen writes that The Hanged Man is about "seeing the same issues as others, but through a different perspective". What the couple has to learn: for each to be self-sufficient; to step out of dependencies, including on each other; to say "no" and set boundaries; to take responsibility for a decision instead of waiting for a push; to look for a shared goal, not only shared time. This card also has a strength in a couple, one the minus hides: tact, attention, the ability to give way, and the ability to sense each other at a distance. The key words are "at a distance".
If there is pressure, threats or fear for one's safety in the couple, this is no longer a question for the cards: it needs a psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

sections.h2: What Waite drew: two towers, a field, a living tree
paragraphs: On Waite's Moon a road runs into the distance between two towers — "the issue into the unknown" — and the dog and the wolf, in his words, are "the fears of the natural mind", guided by "only reflected light". For a couple, the picture holds a detail that is easy to miss: there are two towers, and they do not merge. The road into the unknown runs between them.

In front of Waite's Empress "a field of corn is ripening", and "beyond there is a fall of water". The field has not been reaped — it is ripening. The middle of the tail is the time when the fruit is growing, and it can be neither hurried nor abandoned.

Waite describes The Hanged Man with the precision of a police report: a man hangs head down by one ankle, "the arms are bound behind him, and one leg is crossed over the other". Compare Aristophanes' halves, who froze "throwing their arms about one another". The embrace and the bonds look like opposites but work the same way: the hands are occupied, and nothing can be done with them. Waite adds that the tree is "living wood" and the face "expresses deep entrancement, not suffering". That is the pleasant trap, drawn.

sections.h2: The way out: two who stay two
paragraphs: The way out of the 18-3-12 tail is written in its middle. Diotima describes a lover who raises a shared "third thing" together with the other, "at the touch of the beautiful which is ever present to his memory, even when absent". It is a direct reply to Hephaestus and his "always day and night to be in one another's company". For Diotima the bond rests on shared work and so survives distance; for Aristophanes' halves it rests only on the embrace, and they dare not loosen it even to eat.

The couple's values give the same answer — the point of spiritual purpose, where one reads what the two are meant to walk towards together. In 61.7% of couples with this tail it holds The Hermit, in 38.3% The Moon. And here lies perhaps the quietest clue. The Hermit's beacon, Waite writes, "intimates that 'where I am, you also may be'". The Lovers in the centre he calls "the card of human love, here exhibited as part of the way, the truth and the life". **Both phrases come from one chapter of the Gospel of John, the fourteenth: "I am the way, the truth, and the life" and "that where I am, there ye may be also".** It is a farewell speech: the speaker is leaving and promises that parting will not break the bond. This couple's centre and its most frequent value are described in words about a love that knows how to part. For a couple whose trap is never parting, there could be no better hint.

The Hermit in the values is each partner's right to their own lantern and their own summit. Not "we are one" but "I stand in my own place, and you can come". Where the values hold The Moon, something else is precious: a shared inner world, intuition, the right to a secret. But The Moon too needs a dawn: whatever the two have understood without words is worth putting into words one day.
What this looks like in life:

ul: say aloud what "goes without saying": what one wants, what hurt, what comes next;
keep something of one's own each — an evening, a project, a friend — and talk about it rather than hide it;
choose a shared "third thing" with a beginning and an end: a renovation by autumn, a garden, a project — and see it through;
break a hanging decision into steps: who finds out, who does the sums, by what date;
now and then ask each other Hephaestus's question — "what do you want from me?" — and learn to answer it in words.

paragraphs: The strong version of the 18-3-12 tail is a couple who understand each other without words and still speak in words. Who create rather than only embrace. Who can be apart and still be together. Aristophanes' halves wanted to be melted into one. Diotima's lovers stayed two — and brought a third thing into the world.

Take two people born on the same day, 14 May 1976. Their personal matrix is one and the same. Day — 14, month — 5, year — 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 2 + 3 = 5. Point D: 14 + 5 + 5 = 24 → 6. Centre: 14 + 5 + 5 + 6 = 30 → 3. Tail entry M: 6 + 3 = 9, middle N: 6 + 9 = 15. Each person's karmic tail is 9-15-6.
Now add the same points of the two matrices and reduce the sums to 22 or less:
The couple's centre is 3 + 3 = 6, The Lovers. The couple's values in this example are 18, The Moon.

The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from the two outer numbers: it is the sum of the middles of the two personal tails, 15 + 15. Here the sum of the outer numbers, 18 + 12 = 30 → 3, happens to give the same 3, which is why the same order of numbers also exists as a personal tail — for 1,924 dates since 1900. But the personal 18-3-12 is a different calculation with different roles of the points, and the site has a separate article about it.

sections.h2: 18-3-12 and 18-12-3: the same cards, a different story
paragraphs: The same numbers form one more couple tail — 18-12-3. It is more common, found in 0.539% of couples, and its centre always holds The Devil, 15. There The Hanged Man is the road and The Empress the main task: the couple first gets stuck and only then learns to create something shared. In 18-3-12 the shared thing is created along the way, the main test is not to freeze inside it, and the atmosphere is held by The Lovers rather than The Devil.

ul: **The Moon — entry to the task.** What the two want together: to recognise "their" person and understand them without words. This wish is how the couple enters its task, and later it is the same wish that keeps them from saying things aloud.
**The Empress — middle of the task.** How the couple travels the road: the two begin to produce — a home, a garden, a business, a shared "third thing" that holds them more firmly than the embrace.

**The Hanged Man — main task.** A test of life on pause. The two hold on to each other so tightly that both have their hands full, and decisions hang for years. The lesson is to stay together without standing still.

intro: What follows is an investigation. The first clues sit in the numbers themselves: in three out of four such couples the partners are doubles by personal tail. More are found in the books of Waite and Benebell Wen, and in Plato's text, which lays itself out across these cards almost without remainder. There are no predictions here: the cards know nothing of events or dates. They describe a plot in which a couple may recognise itself.

faq.q: Is the 18-3-12 tail a bad sign for compatibility?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes a task, not a verdict, and this method gives no compatibility percentages. The Hanged Man in the main task shows where the couple risks freezing, and The Empress in the middle shows the road out: through shared work, not only through the feeling that "we are one whole".

faq.q: How do you know a couple has the 18-3-12 tail?
faq.a: Work out both personal matrices and add the same points: entry to entry, middle to middle, main task to main task, reducing any sum above 22. A quick hint: in 77% of such couples both partners have the personal tail 9-15-6, in 12% the tails are 9-12-3 and 9-18-9, and in 11% they are 12-16-4 and 6-14-8. The easiest way is to enter both dates into the compatibility calculator.

faq.q: Why does the example use two people born on the same day?
faq.a: Because a person born on 14.05.1976 has the personal tail 9-15-6, and two such matrices add up to exactly 18-3-12. This is the most common route to this tail: in three cases out of four the partners have identical personal tails. A shared birthday is not needed for that — an identical tail is enough.

faq.q: What should a couple with the 18-3-12 tail do first?
faq.a: Check what each of them does on their own, and take it back. Say wishes aloud instead of waiting to be guessed. Start a shared "third thing" with a clear end — a project, a home, a business — and see it through. And do not put off for years a decision that is hanging: break it into steps and set a date.

faq.q: How does the couple tail 18-3-12 differ from the personal tail 18-3-12?
faq.a: They are different calculations with different roles of the points. A personal tail is calculated from one birth date and speaks about a person. A couple's tail is the sum of the points of two personal matrices, and its three cards are read as the entry to a shared task, the middle of the road and the union's main task. Matching numbers do not make them one story.

report: The most famous story about an "other half" has an ending that almost nobody remembers. In Plato's Symposium, the comic poet Aristophanes tells how Zeus cut the round people in two and the halves rushed to each other. "Throwing their arms about one another, entwined in mutual embraces", they stayed that way — and "were on the point of dying from hunger and self-neglect, because they did not like to do anything apart". The couple tail 18-3-12 tells this myth in three cards. The Moon at the entry is the wish to find one's other half. The Empress in the middle is the road on which the embrace becomes shared work. The Hanged Man in the main task is a test of life on pause.

In Aristophanes, people made of two different halves were children of the Moon, "which is made up of sun and earth". Benebell Wen describes the theme of this card with the words "duality, and dichotomy". And "dichotomy" in Greek means "cutting in two": Plato's Zeus uses the very same words when he splits people apart. In astronomy, it is the name of the phase when exactly half of the Moon's disc is lit. **At the entry to this tail stands a half-moon.**

The entry is what the couple wants together: its common language and its agreements. Here the common language is a language of guesses. At their first meeting the two recognise each other as if they had always known each other, finish each other's sentences, talk until dawn. Aristophanes notes that such lovers "could not explain what they desire of one another": the soul of each has "only a dark and doubtful presentiment". Each, in his words, is looking for their "indenture" — in Greek a "symbolon", half of a broken tally by which a host and a guest recognised each other years later.

The contract between halves has a flaw: no one has ever read it aloud. "A true other half would guess" — and instead of a conversation, the reading of silences begins. One imagines what the other thought and takes offence at what was imagined. The image of the first months does not survive daylight. This is how The Moon at the entry turns into resistance.

report.h3: The trouble and the way out share one word

report: The halves perish of "argia". In Greek it means idleness, and literally work-less-ness: "a-" means "without", "ergon" means "work". Zeus, taking pity, finds a second remedy: the embrace begins to bear fruit, and people "go their ways to the business of life". The original uses the same root — "to their works". Waite's divinatory list for The Empress opens with "Fruitfulness, action, initiative" — exactly what the embracing halves lacked.

The Symposium itself supplies the second half of the answer. A wise woman from Mantinea, Diotima, argues with Aristophanes: lovers seek "neither for the half of themselves, nor for the whole, unless the half or the whole be also a good". For her, love is "birth in beauty, whether of body or soul", and the children she means include poems and laws. The lover "in company with him tends that which he brings forth" — and so such people "have a closer friendship". **The union is held together not by the embrace but by a third thing the two create together.** For a couple this is a home made of a rented flat, a country plot, a shared business, a renovation, a dog, a book — provided each keeps a calling of their own. Diotima described the minus of the middle in a single sentence: a being that "holds what it has conceived and carries it with difficulty". These are plans that stay plans for years, and a home that is always "being got ready".

report.h3: A net the lovers ask for

report: The Hanged Man in the main task is the halves frozen in an embrace. They do not quarrel. They simply stop doing anything apart. Five years in, neither remembers what they liked doing on their own. A move, a wedding, a new job hang for years, because each waits for the other to want it first. One holds everything together and hears reproaches, yet cannot leave: "without me it will all fall apart".

At the end of the speech Aristophanes brings Hephaestus to the lovers. The smith offers to melt the two into one, so that they would be "always day and night" in each other's company. Not one of them, Aristophanes assures his listeners, would refuse. Hephaestus is no random choice: in the Odyssey he had already chained Ares and Aphrodite to a bed with a net so strong that they "could neither get up nor stir hand or foot". In the Symposium the lovers ask for the same net themselves.

**The trap of the 18-3-12 tail is that it is pleasant.** A frozen couple feels fine, so the standstill is hard to notice: no one suffers, things simply stop happening. The lesson here is for each to stay self-sufficient, to step out of dependence on each other, to take responsibility for a decision instead of waiting for a push from outside. The Hanged Man in a couple also has a strength: tact, attention and the ability to sense each other at a distance.
If there is pressure, threats or fear for one's safety in the couple, this is no longer a question for the cards: it needs a psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

report.h3: A love that knows how to part

report: Diotima describes a lover for whom the beloved is "ever present to his memory, even when absent". It is a direct reply to Hephaestus. In the values of such couples The Hermit stands most often, and his beacon, Waite writes, "intimates that 'where I am, you also may be'". The Lovers in the centre Waite calls love "exhibited as part of the way, the truth and the life". Both phrases come from one farewell chapter of the Gospel of John: the speaker is leaving and promises that parting will not break the bond. **This union is described in words about a love that knows how to part.**

The strong version of the tail is two people who understand each other without words and still speak in words: what one wants, what hurt, what comes next. Who create rather than only embrace. Aristophanes' halves wanted to be melted into one. Diotima's lovers stayed two — and brought a third thing into the world.

unit.title: From embrace to shared work

captions.M: Recognise your other half and understand without words
captions.N: Turn the embrace into a home, shared work and fruit
captions.D: Don't freeze together while decisions hang for years

unit.meaning: Wordless intuition brings you together, but what you create together holds you — the key is not to freeze in the embrace.
